abstract: Brain organoids and other model neuronal networks build synaptic circuits through self-organization, and different protocols yield markedly different architectures, letting us test how collective dynamics depend on large-scale organization. We compared organoids of layered cortical-like structure against networks of cell-body clusters joined by axonal cables, quantifying the reproducible patterns of population activity in each. Bursts occurred in both architectures and comprised several collective patterns in each, so no single recurring template describes them. Recurrent activation sequences capture only part of this organization, sequence participation is graded, and neurons that rarely join a sequence still contribute to the shared dynamics. The patterns also pick out overlapping neuronal groups with propagation-like spatial order. Although the patterns differed between tissue models, their organization was conserved, and remained unchanged under pharmacological increases in network activity. Recurrent sequences therefore represent one manifestation of a broader collective organization that emerges across distinct self-organized neural architectures.
